metadata.title: Rotation Numbers of Elements in Thompson's Group ${\bf T}$

extraction_notes.note: finalize warns DP20 introduces two symbols; the 'Let ... Let ... Then' sentences only set up $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\Delta'$ for the simple-split definition, so they were kept in one self-contained definition node (with the 'One checks' claim ClP12 nested inside) rather than split.

The definition of a standard dyadic interval lives in a footnote inside a sentence of the construction AP1; emitted as a nested definition whose statement is the footnote text, which finalize flags as starting mid-sentence.

The local construction of $\phi$ (facets to endpoints, then inductive averaging) is an inductive definition; typed algorithm with two unmarked steps, while the sector-wise globalization was kept as a definition.
Remark 1 describes an algorithm for computing rotation numbers; kept as a remark since it only points to steps carried out in the earlier proofs.

The regularity of $F(\Delta)$ is stated twice (Sections 2 and 3); the Section 2 copy is the claim node, while the Section 3 copy was emitted as a definition node because it introduces the notation $F(\Delta):=\{F(\sigma)\}$ used afterwards.

The sentence 'To see that $\phi$ conjugates ... it suffices to verify the following additional fact' reduces an unstated equivalence of the two realizations of T to ClP11; with no separately stated result it was not made a proof node. The convention 'From now on, $F$ will always denote a piecewise linear automorphism' was also left out.

Theorem A is the cited Ghys-Sergiescu result (origin external) whose two parts the paper re-proves separately; parts I and II are nested external claims, each the target of the paper's proof (PP6, PP7).

nodes.name: Thompson's group T
nodes.statement: One of these $\mathbf{T}$, which will be the subject of this article, is the group of `dyadic' circle homeomorphisms $f:\mathbb{S}^1\to \mathbb{S}^1$. That is, if one takes $\mathbb{S}^1$ to be the interval $[0,1]$ with endpoints identified, then \begin{itemize} \item $f$ preserves the set of dyadic rational numbers (i.e., numbers of the form $p\cdot2^q$, $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$), \item $f$ is linear except at a finite number of dyadic rational points, \item on each interval such that $f$ is linear, the derivative (i.e., slope) is a power of $2$. \end{itemize}
differentia: $f$ preserves the set of dyadic rational numbers (i.e., numbers of the form $p\cdot2^q$, $p,q\in\mathbb{Z}$),
$f$ is linear except at a finite number of dyadic rational points,
on each interval such that $f$ is linear, the derivative (i.e., slope) is a power of $2$.
nodes.statement_short: T is the group of circle homeomorphisms of [0,1]/~ preserving dyadic rationals, piecewise linear with finitely many dyadic breaks and slopes powers of 2.

nodes.name: rotation number
nodes.statement: The \emph{rotation number} \cite{KH} of an orientation preserving circle homeomorphism $f:\mathbb{S}^1\to \mathbb{S}^1$ is the quantity \[ \rho(f)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\widetilde{f}^n(x)}{n} \mod \mathbb{Z}, \] where $\widetilde{f}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is any lift of $f$ to the universal cover $\mathbb{R}$, and $x\in\mathbb{R}$ is any initial point.
nodes.statement_short: Rotation number $\rho(f)$ = limit of $\widetilde f^n(x)/n$ mod $\mathbb{Z}$ for a lift $\widetilde f$ of $f$.

nodes.name: Well-definedness of the rotation number
nodes.statement: Modulo $\mathbb{Z}$, the limit does not depend on the choices of $\widetilde{f}$ and $x$, and it is an important dynamical invariant for $f$.
conclusions: the limit does not depend on the choices of $\widetilde{f}$ and $x$

nodes.name: Rational rotation number iff periodic point
nodes.statement: In particular $\rho(f)$ is rational if and only if $f$ has a periodic point.
conclusions: $\rho(f)$ is rational if and only if $f$ has a periodic point

nodes.name: Theorem A (Ghys-Sergiescu)
nodes.statement: \mbox{} \begin{itemize} \item[I.] For every element $f$ in Thompson's group ${\bf T}$, the rotation number $\rho(f)$ is rational. \item[II.] For every rational number $r$, there is an element $f\in{\bf T}$ such that $\rho(f)=r\mod\mathbb{Z}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Every element of Thompson's group T has rational rotation number, and every rational number occurs as one.
conclusions: the rotation number $\rho(f)$ is rational
there is an element $f\in{\bf T}$ such that $\rho(f)=r\mod\mathbb{Z}$

nodes.name: Theorem A, part I
nodes.statement: For every element $f$ in Thompson's group ${\bf T}$, the rotation number $\rho(f)$ is rational.
assumptions: For every element $f$ in Thompson's group ${\bf T}$
conclusions: the rotation number $\rho(f)$ is rational

nodes.name: Theorem A, part II
nodes.statement: For every rational number $r$, there is an element $f\in{\bf T}$ such that $\rho(f)=r\mod\mathbb{Z}$.
conclusions: there is an element $f\in{\bf T}$ such that $\rho(f)=r\mod\mathbb{Z}$

nodes.name: non-negative reals $\mathbb{R}_+$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{R}_+:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\,x\ge 0\}$ denote the set of non-negative real numbers.

nodes.name: ray
nodes.statement: A {\em ray} in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a rational one dimensional cone, i.e. a set of the form $\tau=\mathbb{R}_+ v$ for some $v\in\mathbb{Z}^2\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}$.
differentia: a set of the form $\tau=\mathbb{R}_+ v$ for some $v\in\mathbb{Z}^2\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}$

nodes.name: generator of a ray
nodes.statement: The first lattice point $v\in\tau\cap(\mathbb{Z}^2\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\})$ is called the \emph{generator} of $\tau$.

nodes.name: real ray
nodes.statement: We will call one dimensional cones with (possibly) irrational slope \emph{real rays}.

nodes.name: sector
nodes.statement: A {\em sector} is a rational two dimensional cone, i.e. a convex set $\sigma = \mathbb{R}_+ v_1 + \mathbb{R}_+ v_2$ for some $v_1,v_2\in\mathbb{Z}^2\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}$ linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$.
differentia: a convex set $\sigma = \mathbb{R}_+ v_1 + \mathbb{R}_+ v_2$ for some $v_1,v_2\in\mathbb{Z}^2\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}$ linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: facets of a sector
nodes.statement: The rays $\tau_i = \mathbb{R}_+ v_i$, $i=1,2$, bounding $\sigma$ are called {\em facets} of $\sigma$.

nodes.name: regular sector
nodes.statement: The sector $\sigma$ is \emph{regular} if the generators $v_1,v_2$ of the facets of $\sigma$ form a basis for $\mathbb{Z}^2$, i.e. if $|\det[v_1\ v_2]|= 1$.
differentia: the generators $v_1,v_2$ of the facets of $\sigma$ form a basis for $\mathbb{Z}^2$, i.e. if $|\det[v_1\ v_2]|= 1$

nodes.name: fan
nodes.statement: A \emph{fan} $\Delta$ is a set of cones consisting of the zero-dimensional cone $\{\mathbf{0}\}$, a finite sequence of rays $\tau_0,\tau_1,\cdots,\tau_d$ given in counterclockwise order, and the intervening sectors $\sigma_j$ bounded by $\tau_{j-1}$ and $\tau_j$, $1\leq j\leq d$.
differentia: a finite sequence of rays $\tau_0,\tau_1,\cdots,\tau_d$ given in counterclockwise order
the intervening sectors $\sigma_j$ bounded by $\tau_{j-1}$ and $\tau_j$, $1\leq j\leq d$
nodes.statement_short: A fan is $\{0\}$ plus a counterclockwise sequence of rays and the sectors between consecutive rays.

nodes.name: support of a fan
nodes.statement: The support of $\Delta$, denoted $\mathrm{supp}(\Delta)$, is the union of all cones in $\Delta$.

nodes.name: Fans are complete
nodes.statement: We assume throughout that our fans are \emph{complete}, i.e. i.e., the sectors $\sigma_j$ in $\Delta$ cover $\mathbb{R}^2$ (hence $\tau_0 = \tau_d$).

nodes.name: regular fan
nodes.statement: A fan is {\em regular} if all its sectors are regular.

nodes.name: piecewise linear map
nodes.statement: A continuous map $F:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is {\em piecewise linear} if there exists a fan $\Delta$ with sectors $\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_d$ and linear transformations $L_i:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $i=1,\cdots,d$ such that $F|_{\sigma_i}=L_i|_{\sigma_i}$ for all $i=1,\cdots,d$.
differentia: there exists a fan $\Delta$ with sectors $\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_d$ and linear transformations $L_i:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $i=1,\cdots,d$ such that $F|_{\sigma_i}=L_i|_{\sigma_i}$ for all $i=1,\cdots,d$
nodes.statement_short: F is piecewise linear if it agrees with a linear map on each sector of some fan.

nodes.name: compatible fan
nodes.statement: Any fan satisfying the above condition is said to be {\em compatible} with $F$.

nodes.name: Orientation of a piecewise linear map
nodes.statement: The map $F$ is orientation preserving if and only if each of $L_i$ is.
conclusions: The map $F$ is orientation preserving if and only if each of $L_i$ is.

nodes.name: piecewise linear automorphism of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement: A {\em piecewise linear automorphism of $\mathbb{Z}^2$} is an orientation preserving, piecewise linear homeomorphism $F:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $F(\mathbb{Z}^2)=\mathbb{Z}^2$.

nodes.name: Linear pieces lie in SL(2,Z)
nodes.statement: If $F$ is a piecewise linear automorphism, then all the maps $L_i$ in the definition must have $\det(L_i)=1$, i.e., $L_i\in \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$.
conclusions: all the maps $L_i$ in the definition must have $\det(L_i)=1$, i.e., $L_i\in \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$

nodes.name: Image of a regular compatible fan is regular
nodes.statement: It follows that if $\Delta$ is a regular fan compatible with $F$, then the fan $F(\Delta)$ obtained by mapping forward all cones in $\Delta$ is also regular, though it is not necessarily compatible with $F$.
assumptions: $\Delta$ is a regular fan compatible with $F$
conclusions: the fan $F(\Delta)$ obtained by mapping forward all cones in $\Delta$ is also regular, though it is not necessarily compatible with $F$

nodes.name: Projectivization of piecewise linear homeomorphisms
nodes.statement: Every piecewise linear homeomorphism $F:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ induces a circle homeomorphism by projectivizing.
conclusions: induces a circle homeomorphism by projectivizing

nodes.name: set of real rays $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: More precisely, $F$ permutes the set ${\mathcal{R}}$ of real rays in $\mathbb{R}^2$, which are parameterized by $\mathbb{S}^1$.

nodes.name: Circle map determines the automorphism
nodes.statement: If, moreover, $F$ restricts to a bijection $\mathbb{Z}^2\to\mathbb{Z}^2$, then the induced homeomorphism of $\mathbb{S}^1$ completely determines $F$.
conclusions: the induced homeomorphism of $\mathbb{S}^1$ completely determines $F$

nodes.name: Local construction of the conjugacy $\phi:{\mathcal{R}}_\sigma\to I$
nodes.statement: Let $I = [\frac{a}{2^k},\frac{a+1}{2^k}]$ be a ``dyadic standard\footnote{A dyadic sub-interval $I\subset[0,1]$ is called {\em standard} if it is of the form $I = [\frac{a}{2^k},\frac{a+1}{2^k}]$. For example, the interval $[\frac 1 4,\frac 1 2]$ is dyadic and standard, whereas $[\frac 1 4,\frac 3 4]$ is dyadic but not standard. }'' interval and $\sigma\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a regular sector generated by the (oriented) basis $v_1,v_2\subset \mathbb{Z}^2$. Taking ${\mathcal{R}}_\sigma\subset {\mathcal{R}}$ to be the set of real rays in $\sigma$, we define a homeomorphism $\phi:{\mathcal{R}}_\sigma\to I$ as follows, identifying each rational ray with its generator $v\in\mathbb{Z}^2$. We first assign facets to endpoints: $\phi(v_1) = \frac{a}{2^k}$ and $\phi(v_2) = \frac{a+1}{2^k}$. Then we proceed inductively by averaging: $\phi(v_1+v_2) = \frac12(\phi(v_1) + \phi(v_2))$, and more generally, if $\phi$ is defined at two primitive points (i.e. integral points where the two coordinates are coprime) $v,v'\in\sigma\cap \mathbb{Z}^2$ but at no points in the intervening sector, then we set $\phi(v+v') = \frac12(\phi(v)+\phi(v'))$.
input: ``dyadic standard\footnote{A dyadic sub-interval $I\subset[0,1]$ is called {\em standard} if it is of the form $I = [\frac{a}{2^k},\frac{a+1}{2^k}]$. For example, the interval $[\frac 1 4,\frac 1 2]$ is dyadic and standard, whereas $[\frac 1 4,\frac 3 4]$ is dyadic but not standard. }'' interval
$\sigma\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a regular sector generated by the (oriented) basis $v_1,v_2\subset \mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Builds $\phi$ from rays of a regular sector to a standard dyadic interval: facets go to endpoints, then mediants $v+v'$ go to midpoints, inductively.

nodes.name: standard dyadic interval
nodes.statement: A dyadic sub-interval $I\subset[0,1]$ is called {\em standard} if it is of the form $I = [\frac{a}{2^k},\frac{a+1}{2^k}]$. For example, the interval $[\frac 1 4,\frac 1 2]$ is dyadic and standard, whereas $[\frac 1 4,\frac 3 4]$ is dyadic but not standard.

nodes.name: Assign facets to endpoints
nodes.statement: We first assign facets to endpoints: $\phi(v_1) = \frac{a}{2^k}$ and $\phi(v_2) = \frac{a+1}{2^k}$.

nodes.name: Inductive averaging
nodes.statement: Then we proceed inductively by averaging: $\phi(v_1+v_2) = \frac12(\phi(v_1) + \phi(v_2))$, and more generally, if $\phi$ is defined at two primitive points (i.e. integral points where the two coordinates are coprime) $v,v'\in\sigma\cap \mathbb{Z}^2$ but at no points in the intervening sector, then we set $\phi(v+v') = \frac12(\phi(v)+\phi(v'))$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly send the sum $v+v'$ of adjacent already-assigned primitive points to the midpoint of their images.

nodes.name: Local $\phi$ is an orientation-preserving homeomorphism
nodes.statement: One checks that this procedure results in an order-preserving bijection between rational rays in $\sigma$ and dyadic points in $I$ which therefore extends to an orientation-preserving homeomorphism $\phi:{\mathcal{R}}_\sigma \to I$.
conclusions: this procedure results in an order-preserving bijection between rational rays in $\sigma$ and dyadic points in $I$ which therefore extends to an orientation-preserving homeomorphism $\phi:{\mathcal{R}}_\sigma \to I$

nodes.name: Minkowski's question mark function
nodes.statement: Note that when $I=[0,1]$ and $\sigma$ is the cone generated by $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with ${\mathcal{R}}_\sigma$ parameterized by the slope, $\phi$ is known as \emph{Minkowski's question mark function}.

nodes.name: global conjugacy $\phi:{\mathcal{R}}\to[0,1]$
nodes.statement: One globalizes $\phi$ by choosing any partition $\mathbb{R}^2 = \sigma_1\cup\dots\cup\sigma_d$ into regular sectors and a corresponding partition $[0,1]=I_1\cup\dots\cup I_d$ into standard dyadic intervals and defining $\phi|_{{\mathcal{R}}_{\sigma_j}}:{\mathcal{R}}_{\sigma_j}\to I_j$ sector-wise as above.
nodes.statement_short: Global $\phi$: partition the plane into regular sectors and [0,1] into standard dyadic intervals, and apply the local construction sector-wise.

nodes.name: Local compatibility of $\phi$ with SL(2,Z)
nodes.statement: Let $\phi:{\mathcal{R}}_\sigma \to I$ be the `local' version of $\phi$ defined above. Let $\sigma'$ be another regular sector, $I'$ another standard dyadic interval, and $\phi':{\mathcal{R}}_{\sigma'}\to I'$ the analogous homeomorphism. Then $\phi'\circ F = f\circ \phi$ where $F\in \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ is the unique element such that $F(\sigma) = \sigma'$ and $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is the unique increasing affine map such that $f(I) = I'$.
assumptions: Let $\phi:{\mathcal{R}}_\sigma \to I$ be the `local' version of $\phi$ defined above.
Let $\sigma'$ be another regular sector, $I'$ another standard dyadic interval, and $\phi':{\mathcal{R}}_{\sigma'}\to I'$ the analogous homeomorphism.
conclusions: $\phi'\circ F = f\circ \phi$ where $F\in \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ is the unique element such that $F(\sigma) = \sigma'$ and $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is the unique increasing affine map such that $f(I) = I'$
nodes.statement_short: The local maps $\phi,\phi'$ intertwine the SL(2,Z) map taking $\sigma$ to $\sigma'$ with the affine map taking $I$ to $I'$.

nodes.name: refinement of a fan
nodes.statement: A \emph{refinement} of a fan $\Delta$ is a fan $\Delta'$ with the same support as $\Delta$ and such that for every cone $\sigma'\in\Delta'$, there exists $\sigma\in\Delta$ such that $\sigma'\subseteq\sigma$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.genus: fan $\Delta'$ with the same support as $\Delta$
differentia: for every cone $\sigma'\in\Delta'$, there exists $\sigma\in\Delta$ such that $\sigma'\subseteq\sigma$

nodes.name: Existence of regular refinements
nodes.statement: Any fan admits a regular refinement.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
conclusions: Any fan admits a regular refinement.
nodes.label: lem:regularization

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that any sector $\sigma$ may be partitioned into regular sectors. If $\sigma$ is not regular, then the ray generators $u_1,u_2$ of its facets must satisfy $|\det[u_1\ u_2]|\ge 2$. This implies that there must be at least one primitive point $w$ in the interior of the parallelogram formed by $u_1$ and $u_2$. The ray $\mathbb{R}_+ w$ divides $\sigma$ into two new sectors. Since $|\det[w\ u_i]| < |\det[u_1\ u_2]|$, $i=1,2$, we see that finitely many such subdivisions will result in a partition of $\sigma$ into regular sectors.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Subdivide each non-regular sector by a primitive point in its fundamental parallelogram; the determinant strictly decreases, so the process terminates.

nodes.name: simple split of a fan
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma\in\Delta$ be a regular sector with its boundary rays generated by $u_1,u_2\in\mathbb{Z}^2$. Let $\tau\subset \sigma$ be the ray generated by some point $u\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ in the interior of $\sigma$. Then $\sigma\setminus\tau$ is a union of two disjoint sectors $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$. One checks that they are both regular if and only if $u=u_1+u_2$. We then call the fan $\Delta'=(\Delta\setminus\{\sigma\})\cup\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\tau\}$ the {\em simple split} of $\Delta$ at $\sigma$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Splitting a regular sector by the ray through $u_1+u_2$ (the only split keeping both halves regular) gives the simple split.

nodes.name: Regular splits occur only at $u_1+u_2$
nodes.statement: One checks that they are both regular if and only if $u=u_1+u_2$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
conclusions: they are both regular if and only if $u=u_1+u_2$

nodes.name: Simple splits preserve regularity
nodes.statement: If $\Delta$ is regular then so is $\Delta'$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
conclusions: so is $\Delta'$

nodes.name: simple merge of a fan
nodes.statement: Conversely, we call $\Delta$ the {\em simple merge} of $\Delta'$ at $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$

nodes.name: Regular refinements via simple splits
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\Delta,\Delta'$ are regular fans, and $\Delta'$ refines $\Delta$. Then one can obtain $\Delta'$ from $\Delta$ by a sequence of simple splits.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
conclusions: one can obtain $\Delta'$ from $\Delta$ by a sequence of simple splits
nodes.label: lem:regular_refinement

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: We need to consider only the case where $\Delta$ is the fan determined by a single regular sector $\sigma := \mathbb{R}_+ u + \mathbb{R}_+ v$. Working inductively, it suffices to show that either $\Delta'$ includes the ray $\tau := \mathbb{R}_+ (u+v)$ that barycentrically subdivies $\sigma$, or $\Delta' = \Delta$. If $\tau \notin \Delta'$, then we let $\tau_1 = \mathbb{R}_+(au + bv)$, $\tau_2 = \mathbb{R}_+(cu + dv)$ be the facets of the sector $\sigma' \in \Delta'$ that contains $\tau$. We may assume that $a > b\geq 0$ and $d> c\geq 0$ are all integers. Since $\sigma'$ is regular, we get $$ 1 = ad-bc \geq (b+1)(c+1) - bc = b+c+1. $$ Thus $b=c = 0$ and $a=d=1$, i.e. $\sigma' = \sigma$ and $\Delta' = \Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a single regular sector and induct: either the refinement contains the barycentric ray $u+v$, or a determinant inequality forces it to be trivial.

nodes.name: image fan $F(\Delta)$
nodes.statement: Note that if $\Delta$ is a regular fan compatible with $F$, then the image fan $F(\Delta) :=\{F(\sigma):\sigma\in \Delta\}$ is also regular.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$

nodes.name: isomorphism of fans
nodes.statement: If $\Delta'$ is another regular fan, then we say that $F$ is an {\em isomorphism} from $\Delta$ to $\Delta'$ if $F(\Delta) = \Delta'$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$

nodes.name: simple split / simple merge map
nodes.statement: Similarly, we say that $F$ is a {\em simple split} or {\em simple merge} of $\Delta'$ if $F(\Delta)$ is accordingly, a simple split or simple merge of $\Delta'$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$

nodes.name: simple map
nodes.statement: We call $F$ a {\em simple} map from $\Delta$ to $\Delta'$ if $F$ is of one of these three types.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
differentia: $F$ is of one of these three types

nodes.name: approximate map $F_\sharp$
nodes.statement: Regardless, we associate to $F$ a partially defined, `approximate' map $F_\sharp:\Delta\to\Delta'$ as follows: for each $\sigma\in\Delta$, we take $F_\sharp\sigma$ to be the smallest cone in $\Delta'$ containing $F(\sigma)$. If no single cone in $\Delta'$ contains $F(\sigma)$, then we leave $F_\sharp\sigma$ undefined.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: $F_\sharp\sigma$ is the smallest cone of $\Delta'$ containing $F(\sigma)$, undefined if none exists.

nodes.name: Domain of definition of $F_\sharp$
nodes.statement: Hence $F_\sharp\tau$ is defined for all rays $\tau\in\Delta$, though the image might be a sector or a ray; whereas for each sector $\sigma\in\Delta$, the cone $F_\sharp \sigma$ is either another sector or undefined.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
conclusions: $F_\sharp\tau$ is defined for all rays $\tau\in\Delta$, though the image might be a sector or a ray
for each sector $\sigma\in\Delta$, the cone $F_\sharp \sigma$ is either another sector or undefined

nodes.name: Functoriality of approximate maps
nodes.statement: If $G$ is another piecewise linear automorphism of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $G_\sharp:\Delta'\to\Delta''$ is an approximate map of fans, then we have $G_\sharp F_\sharp \sigma = (G\circ F)_\sharp\sigma$ provided that the left side is defined.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
assumptions: $G$ is another piecewise linear automorphism of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $G_\sharp:\Delta'\to\Delta''$ is an approximate map of fans
conclusions: $G_\sharp F_\sharp \sigma = (G\circ F)_\sharp\sigma$ provided that the left side is defined

nodes.name: Decomposition into simple maps
nodes.statement: Let $\Delta$ be a regular fan compatible with $F$. Then there is a decomposition $F=f_{n-1}\circ\dots \circ f_0$ into piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and a corresponding sequence of regular fans $\Delta_0,\dots,\Delta_n$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $\Delta_0 = \Delta_n = \Delta$; \item $\Delta_j$ is compatible with $f_j$ for $0\leq j\leq n-1$; \item $f_j$ is a simple map from $\Delta_j$ to $\Delta_{j+1}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
assumptions: $\Delta$ be a regular fan compatible with $F$
conclusions: there is a decomposition $F=f_{n-1}\circ\dots \circ f_0$ into piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and a corresponding sequence of regular fans $\Delta_0,\dots,\Delta_n$
$\Delta_0 = \Delta_n = \Delta$;
$\Delta_j$ is compatible with $f_j$ for $0\leq j\leq n-1$;
$f_j$ is a simple map from $\Delta_j$ to $\Delta_{j+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: A PL automorphism with a regular compatible fan factors as a cycle of simple maps (isomorphism, simple splits, simple merges) between regular fans returning to $\Delta$.
nodes.label: prop:decomposition

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: First, set $f_0=F$ and $\Delta_1=F(\Delta)$. Lemma \ref{lem:regularization} then gives a regular common refinement $\Delta'$ of $\Delta$ and $F(\Delta)$. Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:regular_refinement}, we know that we can obtain $\Delta'$ from $F(\Delta)$ by performing finitely many simple splits, i.e. we have a sequence \[ \xymatrix{ \Delta \ar[rr]^{F} && \Delta_1=F(\Delta) \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta_2 \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta_k=\Delta' } \] in which all but the first arrow represents a simple split; and the first arrow is an isomorphism. Similarly, there is a sequence \[ \xymatrix{ \Delta_k=\Delta' \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta_{k+1} \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta_{n-1} \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta = \Delta_n } \] such that each arrow is a simple merge, $i=k,\cdots,n-1$. Putting the two sequences together completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Map $\Delta$ isomorphically to $F(\Delta)$, split up to a common regular refinement, then merge back down to $\Delta$.

nodes.name: deterministic cone
nodes.statement: We call a cone $\tau\in\Delta$ {\em deterministic} for the approximate self-map $F_\sharp:\Delta\to\Delta$ if all its approximate forward images $(F_\sharp)^j\tau$, $j\ge 1$, are defined.
differentia: all its approximate forward images $(F_\sharp)^j\tau$, $j\ge 1$, are defined

nodes.name: Existence of refinements with deterministic rays
nodes.statement: For any piecewise linear automorphism $F$ and any fan $\Delta$, there exists a regular refinement $\Delta'$ of $\Delta$ such that $\Delta'$ is regular and compatible with $F$, and every ray in $\Delta'$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp:\Delta'\to\Delta'$.
assumptions: any piecewise linear automorphism $F$ and any fan $\Delta$
conclusions: there exists a regular refinement $\Delta'$ of $\Delta$ such that $\Delta'$ is regular and compatible with $F$, and every ray in $\Delta'$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp:\Delta'\to\Delta'$
nodes.statement_short: Every fan has a regular refinement compatible with $F$ in which every ray is deterministic for $F_\sharp$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement:
Let $f_j$ and $\Delta_j$ be the maps and associated fans in the decomposition of $F$ from Proposition ef{prop:decomposition}. Since $\Delta_0 = \Delta_n$, we may extend these sequences of maps/fans periodically, e.g. $f_j := f_{j\mod n}$ for all $j\in\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that there exists a ray $	au\in\Delta$ that is not deterministic for $F_\sharp:\Delta	o\Delta$. In particular, we know $F(\Delta)
eq \Delta$, so $n\geq 2$. Then by replacing $	au$ with an approximate forward image, we may assume that $F_\sharp 	au = \sigma$ is a sector and that $(F_\sharp)^k \sigma$ is undefined for $k\in\mathbb{N}$ large enough. We may refine this observation using the decomposition of $F$. Namely, there exist indices $i < k \in\mathbb{N}$, and a ray $	au_i\in\Delta_i$ such that  egin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\sigma_{i+1} := f_{i\sharp} 	au_i \in \Delta_{i+1}$ is a sector; \item[(ii)] $\sigma_{j+1} := f_{j\sharp}\sigma_j \in \Delta_{j+1}$ is well-defined for $ j =i+1,\cdots, k-1$, but $f_{k\sharp}\sigma_{k}$ is not defined; \item[(iii)] $i,	au_i,k$ are chosen so that $k-i$ is as small as possible given the first two conditions. \end{itemize} That is, we attend to the following sequence: \[ \xymatrix{ 	au_i\in\Delta_{i} \ar[rr]^{f_i} && \sigma_{i+1}\in\Delta_{i+1} \ar[rr]^{f_{i+1}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{f_{k-1}} && \sigma_{k}\in\Delta_k \ar[rr]^{f_k} && \Delta_{k+1} } \] The idea is to inductively refine the fans $\Delta_{i+1},\cdots,\Delta_{k}$ so that $f_k$ becomes an isomorphism. Condition (i) together with the fact that $f_i$ is simple from $\Delta_i$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ means that $	au_{i+1} := f_i(	au_i)$ is the unique ray that divides $\sigma_{i+1}$ into two regular cones. Replacing $\sigma_{i+1}$ with these two cones and adding the ray $	au_{i+1}$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ turns the map $f_i:\Delta_i	o\Delta_{i+1}$ into an isomorphism from $\Delta_i$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$. Note that in this (and succeeding) steps, we apply the same refinement to all fans $\Delta_{i+\ell n}$ equivalent mod $n$ to $\Delta_i$. Since $n\geq 2$ this does not affect the outcome. Turning from $f_i$ to $f_{i+1}$, we find two possible cases. If $i+1=k$, then $f_{i+1}(\sigma_{i+1})$ is equal to the union of two adjacent sectors in $\Delta_{i+2}$. Since the above refinement of $\Delta_{i+1}$ split $\sigma_{i+1}$ into two regular cones, $f_{i+1}$ is now an isomorphism from $\Delta_{i+1}$ to $\Delta_{i+2}$. Otherwise, $i+1<k$. If $f_{i+1}$ was initially a merge, then there is another ray $	ilde	au_{i+1}\in\Delta_{i+1}$ such that $f_{i+1}(	ilde	au_{i+1})
otin\Delta_{i+2}$. However, our minimality assumption on $k-i$ guarantees that the images $f_{i+1}(	ilde	au_{i+1})$ and $f_{i+1}(	au_{i+1})$ lie in different sectors. Hence regardless of whether $f_{i+1}$ is a merge or not, $f_{i+1}(	au_{i+1})$ divides $\sigma_{i+2}$ into two \emph{regular} cones. So as with $\Delta_{i+1}$, we can refine $\Delta_{i+2}$ by splitting $\sigma_{i+2}$ into two regular sectors, the result being that $f_{i+1}$ remains a simple map. In this case, we move on to $f_{i+2}$ and repeat the process until we reach $f_k$. In the end, $f_k$ is improved from a split to an isomorphism, and maps $f_j$ with $j
ot\equiv k\mod n$ remain simple of the same type as before. If there remain rays in $\Delta=\Delta_0$ that are not deterministic for $F_\sharp$, then we repeat the process. Since there are only finitely many $f_j$ (modulo $n$), finitely many repetitions leads to a situation in which either all rays in $\Delta$ are deterministic or all $f_j$ are isomorphisms. In the latter case $F$ is itself an isomorphism from $\Delta$ to $\Delta$, and all rays are deterministic anyhow.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the decomposition periodically and pick a non-deterministic ray with $k-i$ minimal; refine the intermediate fans along its orbit so $f_k$ becomes an isomorphism. Repeat; finitely many $f_j$ mod $n$ ensures termination.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A, part I
nodes.statement: Given any piecewise linear automorphism $F$ of $\mathbb{Z}^2$, we first find any fan $\Delta$ such that $\Delta$ is compatible with $F$. Next, we find a regular refinement $\Delta'$ of $\Delta$, then $\Delta'$ is still compatible with $F$. Finally, we find a further refinement $\Delta''$ such that every ray in $\Delta''$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp$. Observe how $F$ acts on the rays and sectors of $\Delta''$, either one of the following will happen: \begin{itemize} \item There is never a ray mapped into a sector, so rays always map to rays, and $F$ is permuting the rays. In this case, some iterate of every ray is going back to itself and $F$ is of finite order. \item There is a ray maps into a sector $\sigma$, then $\sigma$ must be deterministic for $F_\sharp$, and $(F_\sharp)^j \sigma$, $j\ge 1$, are all defined and are sectors. Then again, we have finitely many sectors, there must be some $i<j$ such that $(F_\sharp)^i \sigma=(F_\sharp)^j \sigma$. As a consequence, there is a ray in $(F_\sharp)^i \sigma$ that is fixed by $F^{j-i}$, so the circle map induced by $F$ has a periodic point. \end{itemize} In either case, the rotation number of $F$ is rational because there is a periodic point. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to a refinement with deterministic rays; either $F$ permutes rays (finite order) or some sector's orbit under $F_\sharp$ cycles, yielding a periodic ray, so $\rho$ is rational.

nodes.name: Algorithm for computing rotation numbers
nodes.statement: Our proof also gives an algorithm for finding the rotation number of a piecewise linear automorphism $F$. First, find a fan $\Delta$ that is compatible with $F$. Then find a regular refinement $\Delta'$ of $\Delta$ such that every ray in $\Delta'$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp$. This can be done effectively by Lemma~\ref{lem:regularization}, Lemma~\ref{lem:regular_refinement}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:decomposition}. Tracing the orbit of each ray in $\Delta'$, as we did in the above proof, will locate the sectors containing periodic (real) rays, and this will then give the rotation number of $F$.
nodes.statement_short: The proof yields an effective algorithm: refine a compatible fan until all rays are deterministic, then trace ray orbits to find periodic rays.

nodes.name: Necessity of $F(\mathbb{Z}^2)=\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement: We stress here that in the definition of piecewise linear automorphism, the condition $F(\mathbb{Z}^2)=\mathbb{Z}^2$ is crucial for the Theorem A to hold. If we only require that $F(\mathbb{Z}^2)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^2$, then it is easy to find a linear map, e.g., $F=\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{smallmatrix}\right]$ such that the corresponding circle homeomorphism has an irrational rotation number.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem A fails if only $F(\mathbb{Z}^2)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^2$ is required, e.g. a rotation-scaling by $(4,3)$ has irrational rotation number.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem A, part II
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that for any given integer $n\ge 3$, we can find a piecewise linear automorphism $F$ of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ such that $\rho(F)=1/n$. For each integer $n\ge 3$ we can find a regular fan $\Delta$ with $n$ sectors, say $\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_n=\sigma_0$, arranged in the counterclockwise order. Since each $\sigma_i$ is regular, there is a unique $L_i\in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ such that $L_i$ maps $\sigma_i$ bijectively onto $\sigma_{i+1}$, $i=0,\cdots,n-1$ and maps the lattice points in $\sigma_i$ bijectively onto lattice points in $\sigma_{i+1}$. Define $F$ as $F|_{\sigma_i}=L_i|_{\sigma_i}$, i.e., $F$ is rotating the sectors, sending $\sigma_i$ to $\sigma_{i+1}$. Then $F$ is periodic of period $n$, and therefore $\rho(F)=1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Construction: on a regular fan with $n$ sectors, rotate each sector onto the next by the unique SL(2,Z) map, giving a period-$n$ element with $\rho=1/n$.

nodes.name: Reduce to one sector
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that any sector $\sigma$ may be partitioned into regular sectors.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to partitioning a single sector into regular sectors.

nodes.name: Find an interior primitive point
nodes.statement: If $\sigma$ is not regular, then the ray generators $u_1,u_2$ of its facets must satisfy $|\det[u_1\ u_2]|\ge 2$. This implies that there must be at least one primitive point $w$ in the interior of the parallelogram formed by $u_1$ and $u_2$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: A non-regular sector has determinant at least 2, so its parallelogram contains a primitive point $w$.

nodes.name: Subdivide by the ray through $w$
nodes.statement: The ray $\mathbb{R}_+ w$ divides $\sigma$ into two new sectors.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Split the sector along the ray through $w$.

nodes.name: Termination by determinant decrease
nodes.statement: Since $|\det[w\ u_i]| < |\det[u_1\ u_2]|$, $i=1,2$, we see that finitely many such subdivisions will result in a partition of $\sigma$ into regular sectors.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Determinants strictly decrease, so finitely many subdivisions yield regular sectors.

nodes.name: Reduce to a single sector
nodes.statement: We need to consider only the case where $\Delta$ is the fan determined by a single regular sector $\sigma := \mathbb{R}_+ u + \mathbb{R}_+ v$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the fan of one regular sector.

nodes.name: Inductive reduction
nodes.statement: Working inductively, it suffices to show that either $\Delta'$ includes the ray $\tau := \mathbb{R}_+ (u+v)$ that barycentrically subdivies $\sigma$, or $\Delta' = \Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: By induction, suffices to show $\Delta'$ contains the barycentric ray or equals $\Delta$.

nodes.name: Introduce the containing sector
nodes.statement: If $\tau \notin \Delta'$, then we let $\tau_1 = \mathbb{R}_+(au + bv)$, $\tau_2 = \mathbb{R}_+(cu + dv)$ be the facets of the sector $\sigma' \in \Delta'$ that contains $\tau$. We may assume that $a > b\geq 0$ and $d> c\geq 0$ are all integers.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: If the barycentric ray is absent, write the facets of the sector containing it in the basis $u,v$.

nodes.name: Determinant inequality
nodes.statement: Since $\sigma'$ is regular, we get $$ 1 = ad-bc \geq (b+1)(c+1) - bc = b+c+1. $$
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Regularity gives $1=ad-bc\ge b+c+1$.

nodes.name: Conclude $\Delta'=\Delta$
nodes.statement: Thus $b=c = 0$ and $a=d=1$, i.e. $\sigma' = \sigma$ and $\Delta' = \Delta$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Hence $b=c=0$, so $\sigma'=\sigma$ and $\Delta'=\Delta$.

nodes.name: Common regular refinement
nodes.statement: First, set $f_0=F$ and $\Delta_1=F(\Delta)$. Lemma \ref{lem:regularization} then gives a regular common refinement $\Delta'$ of $\Delta$ and $F(\Delta)$.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Set $f_0=F$ and apply Lemma 3.1 to get a regular common refinement of $\Delta$ and $F(\Delta)$.

nodes.name: Split sequence
nodes.statement: Then by Lemma~\ref{lem:regular_refinement}, we know that we can obtain $\Delta'$ from $F(\Delta)$ by performing finitely many simple splits, i.e. we have a sequence \[ \xymatrix{ \Delta \ar[rr]^{F} && \Delta_1=F(\Delta) \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta_2 \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta_k=\Delta' } \] in which all but the first arrow represents a simple split; and the first arrow is an isomorphism.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.2 reach the refinement from $F(\Delta)$ by simple splits.

nodes.name: Merge sequence and conclude
nodes.statement: Similarly, there is a sequence \[ \xymatrix{ \Delta_k=\Delta' \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta_{k+1} \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta_{n-1} \ar[rr]^{\mathrm{id}} && \Delta = \Delta_n } \] such that each arrow is a simple merge, $i=k,\cdots,n-1$. Putting the two sequences together completes the proof.
nodes.section: 3 Decomposition of piecewise linear automorphisms of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement_short: Merge back down to $\Delta$ by simple merges and concatenate.

nodes.name: Periodic extension and non-deterministic ray
nodes.statement: Let $f_j$ and $\Delta_j$ be the maps and associated fans in the decomposition of $F$ from Proposition \ref{prop:decomposition}. Since $\Delta_0 = \Delta_n$, we may extend these sequences of maps/fans periodically, e.g. $f_j := f_{j\mod n}$ for all $j\in\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that there exists a ray $\tau\in\Delta$ that is not deterministic for $F_\sharp:\Delta\to\Delta$. In particular, we know $F(\Delta)\neq \Delta$, so $n\geq 2$. Then by replacing $\tau$ with an approximate forward image, we may assume that $F_\sharp \tau = \sigma$ is a sector and that $(F_\sharp)^k \sigma$ is undefined for $k\in\mathbb{N}$ large enough.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the decomposition periodically and assume some ray is non-deterministic, reducing to a ray mapping into a sector with eventually undefined image.

nodes.name: Minimal bad chain
nodes.statement: We may refine this observation using the decomposition of $F$. Namely, there exist indices $i < k \in\mathbb{N}$, and a ray $\tau_i\in\Delta_i$ such that \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\sigma_{i+1} := f_{i\sharp} \tau_i \in \Delta_{i+1}$ is a sector; \item[(ii)] $\sigma_{j+1} := f_{j\sharp}\sigma_j \in \Delta_{j+1}$ is well-defined for $ j =i+1,\cdots, k-1$, but $f_{k\sharp}\sigma_{k}$ is not defined; \item[(iii)] $i,\tau_i,k$ are chosen so that $k-i$ is as small as possible given the first two conditions. \end{itemize} That is, we attend to the following sequence: \[ \xymatrix{ \tau_i\in\Delta_{i} \ar[rr]^{f_i} && \sigma_{i+1}\in\Delta_{i+1} \ar[rr]^{f_{i+1}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{f_{k-1}} && \sigma_{k}\in\Delta_k \ar[rr]^{f_k} && \Delta_{k+1} } \]
nodes.statement_short: Choose a ray $\tau_i$ and indices $i<k$ with $k-i$ minimal so the sector chain fails at $f_k$.

nodes.name: Condition (i)
nodes.statement: We may refine this observation using the decomposition of $F$. Namely, there exist indices $i < k \in\mathbb{N}$, and a ray $\tau_i\in\Delta_i$ such that \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\sigma_{i+1} := f_{i\sharp} \tau_i \in \Delta_{i+1}$ is a sector;
nodes.statement_short: Pick indices and a ray whose first image is a sector.

nodes.name: Condition (ii)
nodes.statement: [(ii)] $\sigma_{j+1} := f_{j\sharp}\sigma_j \in \Delta_{j+1}$ is well-defined for $ j =i+1,\cdots, k-1$, but $f_{k\sharp}\sigma_{k}$ is not defined;
nodes.statement_short: Sector images stay defined until $f_k$, where the image is undefined.

nodes.name: Condition (iii): minimality
nodes.statement: [(iii)] $i,\tau_i,k$ are chosen so that $k-i$ is as small as possible given the first two conditions. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Choose the data with $k-i$ minimal.

nodes.name: Display the chain
nodes.statement: That is, we attend to the following sequence: \[ \xymatrix{ \tau_i\in\Delta_{i} \ar[rr]^{f_i} && \sigma_{i+1}\in\Delta_{i+1} \ar[rr]^{f_{i+1}} &&\cdots \ar[rr]^{f_{k-1}} && \sigma_{k}\in\Delta_k \ar[rr]^{f_k} && \Delta_{k+1} } \]
nodes.statement_short: Record the resulting chain of sectors.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: The idea is to inductively refine the fans $\Delta_{i+1},\cdots,\Delta_{k}$ so that $f_k$ becomes an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: refine intermediate fans so $f_k$ becomes an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Refine $\Delta_{i+1}$
nodes.statement: Condition (i) together with the fact that $f_i$ is simple from $\Delta_i$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ means that $\tau_{i+1} := f_i(\tau_i)$ is the unique ray that divides $\sigma_{i+1}$ into two regular cones. Replacing $\sigma_{i+1}$ with these two cones and adding the ray $\tau_{i+1}$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$ turns the map $f_i:\Delta_i\to\Delta_{i+1}$ into an isomorphism from $\Delta_i$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$. Note that in this (and succeeding) steps, we apply the same refinement to all fans $\Delta_{i+\ell n}$ equivalent mod $n$ to $\Delta_i$. Since $n\geq 2$ this does not affect the outcome.
nodes.statement_short: Add the ray $f_i(\tau_i)$ to $\Delta_{i+1}$, making $f_i$ an isomorphism; do this for all fans equivalent mod $n$.

nodes.name: Case $i+1=k$
nodes.statement: Turning from $f_i$ to $f_{i+1}$, we find two possible cases. If $i+1=k$, then $f_{i+1}(\sigma_{i+1})$ is equal to the union of two adjacent sectors in $\Delta_{i+2}$. Since the above refinement of $\Delta_{i+1}$ split $\sigma_{i+1}$ into two regular cones, $f_{i+1}$ is now an isomorphism from $\Delta_{i+1}$ to $\Delta_{i+2}$.
nodes.statement_short: If $i+1=k$, the split of $\sigma_{i+1}$ makes $f_{i+1}$ an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Case $i+1<k$
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $i+1<k$. If $f_{i+1}$ was initially a merge, then there is another ray $\tilde\tau_{i+1}\in\Delta_{i+1}$ such that $f_{i+1}(\tilde\tau_{i+1})\notin\Delta_{i+2}$. However, our minimality assumption on $k-i$ guarantees that the images $f_{i+1}(\tilde\tau_{i+1})$ and $f_{i+1}(\tau_{i+1})$ lie in different sectors. Hence regardless of whether $f_{i+1}$ is a merge or not, $f_{i+1}(\tau_{i+1})$ divides $\sigma_{i+2}$ into two \emph{regular} cones. So as with $\Delta_{i+1}$, we can refine $\Delta_{i+2}$ by splitting $\sigma_{i+2}$ into two regular sectors, the result being that $f_{i+1}$ remains a simple map. In this case, we move on to $f_{i+2}$ and repeat the process until we reach $f_k$. In the end, $f_k$ is improved from a split to an isomorphism, and maps $f_j$ with $j\not\equiv k\mod n$ remain simple of the same type as before.
nodes.statement_short: If $i+1<k$, minimality ensures the image ray splits $\sigma_{i+2}$ regularly; propagate refinements up to $f_k$.

nodes.name: Iterate and terminate
nodes.statement: If there remain rays in $\Delta=\Delta_0$ that are not deterministic for $F_\sharp$, then we repeat the process. Since there are only finitely many $f_j$ (modulo $n$), finitely many repetitions leads to a situation in which either all rays in $\Delta$ are deterministic or all $f_j$ are isomorphisms. In the latter case $F$ is itself an isomorphism from $\Delta$ to $\Delta$, and all rays are deterministic anyhow.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat; finitely many $f_j$ mod $n$ means the process ends with all rays deterministic.

nodes.name: Build a deterministic refinement
nodes.statement: Given any piecewise linear automorphism $F$ of $\mathbb{Z}^2$, we first find any fan $\Delta$ such that $\Delta$ is compatible with $F$. Next, we find a regular refinement $\Delta'$ of $\Delta$, then $\Delta'$ is still compatible with $F$. Finally, we find a further refinement $\Delta''$ such that every ray in $\Delta''$ is deterministic for $F_\sharp$. Observe how $F$ acts on the rays and sectors of $\Delta''$, either one of the following will happen:
nodes.statement_short: Choose a compatible fan, refine it regularly, then refine so every ray is deterministic (Prop. 4.1).

nodes.name: Case: rays map to rays
nodes.statement: There is never a ray mapped into a sector, so rays always map to rays, and $F$ is permuting the rays. In this case, some iterate of every ray is going back to itself and $F$ is of finite order.
nodes.statement_short: If no ray maps into a sector, $F$ permutes rays and has finite order.

nodes.name: Case: a ray maps into a sector
nodes.statement: There is a ray maps into a sector $\sigma$, then $\sigma$ must be deterministic for $F_\sharp$, and $(F_\sharp)^j \sigma$, $j\ge 1$, are all defined and are sectors. Then again, we have finitely many sectors, there must be some $i<j$ such that $(F_\sharp)^i \sigma=(F_\sharp)^j \sigma$. As a consequence, there is a ray in $(F_\sharp)^i \sigma$ that is fixed by $F^{j-i}$, so the circle map induced by $F$ has a periodic point.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the deterministic sector orbit repeats, giving a ray fixed by $F^{j-i}$, i.e. a periodic point.

nodes.name: Conclude rationality
nodes.statement: In either case, the rotation number of $F$ is rational because there is a periodic point. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Either way there is a periodic point, so the rotation number is rational.

nodes.name: Reduce to $1/n$
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that for any given integer $n\ge 3$, we can find a piecewise linear automorphism $F$ of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ such that $\rho(F)=1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices to realize rotation number $1/n$ for each $n\ge 3$.

nodes.name: Regular fan with $n$ sectors
nodes.statement: For each integer $n\ge 3$ we can find a regular fan $\Delta$ with $n$ sectors, say $\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\cdots,\sigma_n=\sigma_0$, arranged in the counterclockwise order.
nodes.statement_short: Take a regular fan with $n$ sectors.

nodes.name: Linear maps between consecutive sectors
nodes.statement: Since each $\sigma_i$ is regular, there is a unique $L_i\in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ such that $L_i$ maps $\sigma_i$ bijectively onto $\sigma_{i+1}$, $i=0,\cdots,n-1$ and maps the lattice points in $\sigma_i$ bijectively onto lattice points in $\sigma_{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Regularity gives unique SL(2,Z) maps sending each sector to the next.

nodes.name: Define the rotation and conclude
nodes.statement: Define $F$ as $F|_{\sigma_i}=L_i|_{\sigma_i}$, i.e., $F$ is rotating the sectors, sending $\sigma_i$ to $\sigma_{i+1}$. Then $F$ is periodic of period $n$, and therefore $\rho(F)=1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: The resulting $F$ rotates the sectors, has period $n$, so $\rho(F)=1/n$.
